title: Perspectives on astronomy: probing Norwegian pre-service teachers and middle school students
extended_summary:
This paper examines astronomy knowledge, beliefs, and pedagogical perspectives among two Norwegian groups: pre-service science teachers and middle school students. The authors ask whether an adapted astronomy questionnaire can reveal how these groups understand astronomy concepts, how they reason about science-related questions, and whether their responses change before and after astronomy instruction.

To study this, the authors translated and adapted the Introductory Astronomy Questionnaire into Norwegian (the NIAQ) and administered it to pre-service teachers enrolled in Science II at Norway’s largest teacher education institution, as well as to students from eight middle schools in and around Oslo. The teacher sample completed the questionnaire before and after astronomy instruction; the middle school sample was split into a year 8 pre-test group and year 10 post-test group, reflecting their exposure to the standardized astronomy module.

The study reports that pre-service teachers improved on several astronomy explanation tasks after instruction, but also showed an unexpected decline in pedagogical responses when asked how they would answer hypothetical students. Middle school students showed little or no improvement on key astronomy knowledge items between year 8 and year 10, and their scores on distance/size tasks were strongly stratified by gender. The authors conclude that the NIAQ can surface useful insights into astronomy understanding and teaching perspectives, and that some misconceptions persist even after instruction, especially among middle school students.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/observational instrument study with pre/post comparisons, not a randomized controlled trial. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically careful, but evidence credibility is limited by nonrandom samples, descriptive analysis, and ongoing/incomplete reporting of results.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some meaningful conceptual gains for pre-service teachers, but the observed effects are largely descriptive and no effect sizes are reported. The most policy-relevant finding is the decrease in pedagogical responses, which is important but not quantified as a generalizable intervention effect.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports substantial pre/post changes in astronomy conceptual understanding for pre-service teachers, including significant gains in explaining astronomical objects and more complex concepts such as why Earth remains in stable orbit. For middle school students (n=535 year 8 pre-test; n=387 year 10 post-test), however, there was little to no improvement on size/distance reasoning tasks; year 10 scores were statistically identical to or slightly lower than year 8 scores, and many misconceptions remained above 40%-60% prevalence.
finding.measure: Free-response explanations of astronomical objects; ranking tasks on sizes and distances in the universe; multiple-choice astronomy concept responses
finding.study_size: n=41 pre-service teachers; n=535 year 8 students; n=387 year 10 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that pre-service teachers’ positive views of physics and astronomy started high and did not change significantly pre- to post-instruction. For middle school students, similarly high baseline opinions about how interesting and important physics/astronomy are also showed no significant change after instruction.
finding.measure: Likert-style ratings of interest in physics/astronomy, perceived importance to society, and belief that there is more to discover
finding.study_size: n=41 pre-service teachers; n=535 year 8 students; n=387 year 10 students

finding.finding_summary: On prompts asking pre-service teachers what they would say to hypothetical year 10 students, pedagogical responses dropped sharply after instruction: more than one-third were pedagogical pre-instruction, but fewer than 10% were pedagogical post-instruction, with the remainder mostly authoritative. This suggests a deterioration in student-centered explanatory stance after the course rather than improvement.
finding.measure: Categorization of free-response explanations as pedagogical vs authoritative
